title: Arnold raises tutorial
summary: NH demonstrates the 'Arnold raise' (Powell raise), a unilateral lying raise off a bench for lateral and rear delts. He stresses light weight, thumbless grip, a big stretch below the bench, slow negatives and caution because of the shoulder's vulnerability at end range.
claims: Lateral and rear delts are usually undertrained by naturals; hitting them regularly gives capped, 3D shoulders
NH prefers Arnold raises to bent-over lateral raises because the latter recruit too much trap, which overpowers his rear delts
The rear delt responds very well to a stretch
Use a thumbless grip on raises to reduce forearm and wrist involvement and better activate the shoulders
The shoulder's huge mobility is also its weak point: it is weak at the extremes of its range, so big-ROM shoulder work needs care
Do Arnold raises light for 8-12 easy reps, never heavy or low-rep maxes
Standing raises are limited at the bottom by the body; lying on a bench removes that block so the shoulder can overextend, so start light
Don't do this lift cold; do it after a warm-up
The negative and the bottom stretch give the most gains on this lift
Unilateral movements allow better focus and mind-muscle connection than bilateral ones
Once mastered with strict form, momentum can be used for forced negatives, but careful as swinging risks the shoulder
Rear delts don't need huge volume: 4-8 sets a week of 8-12 reps brings visible change
NH's rear delts went from nonexistent to visibly developed with this lift
exercises: lie on bench side, arm cushions body; thumbless grip; raise until rear and medial delt flex; slow negative; let arm stretch under bench without hitting it; shift hips and tilt head to clear the bench
stretch-focused medial/rear delt isolation with less trap than bent-over raises
recruits too much upper trap for NH
